summary:
Borno State stands under Nigeria's national framework, and its criminalisation of same-sex conduct rests independently on Borno's own legislation. The state's statute on prostitution, homosexuality, brothels and other sexual immoralities was signed by Governor Kachalla on 10 December 2000 and gazetted in Borno State Gazette No. 42 Vol. 26 on 18 October 2001. Section 3 makes engaging in prostitution, lesbianism, a homosexual act or pimping an offence in the state. Section 7 provides that any person who 'engages in sexual intercourse with another person of the same gender shall upon conviction be punished with death'. Section 4 deems all brothels closed on commencement, and Section 9 assigns jurisdiction over the statute's offences to the Upper Sharia Courts, Area Courts and Magistrate Courts.

Borno enacted a second, parallel layer of its own. Human Rights Watch's 2004 report lists Borno among the twelve northern Nigerian states that had adopted Shari'a into their criminal legislation by 2002, with Shari'a courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond federal law. The sourcebook of enacted Shari'a Penal Codes records a Borno State Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, signed into law on 3 March 2003, with no operation date or gazette identified; the Borno text was obtained only in May 2006, after the volume's annotation had been completed, which is why Borno is not among the individually annotated codes. The parallel Shari'a layer for Borno therefore rests on a Borno-specific enactment rather than on federal or umbrella coverage.

The UK Home Office country-of-origin information note of June 2025 states that Islamic law applies to Muslims in the twelve northern states and criminalises same-sex sexual acts both between men and between women; the maximum penalty for 'sodomy' for men is death in all twelve states, and penalties for 'lesbianism' range from death to flogging and imprisonment. The note carries a dedicated section on enforcement of Shari'a provisions and on the attitude of the hisbah, the morality police. A visitor to Borno therefore faces two state-level regimes, one secular and one Shari'a-based, each of which independently reaches same-sex conduct, and the secular statute's own jurisdiction clause routes those cases to Shari'a and Area Courts as well as to Magistrate Courts.
tangentialFactors:
Borno's exposure is set by two enactments made by the state itself rather than by the national statute alone: the 2000 morality law, gazetted in 2001, and the Sharia Penal Code Law signed on 3 March 2003. Both are Borno-specific, so the death penalty available in Borno does not depend on how the national framework is applied in the state.

The hisbah, Borno's morality police, is named in the June 2025 UK Home Office note as a body whose attitude forms part of the enforcement picture for Shari'a provisions in the northern states. Enforcement of the state's morality statute is assigned to Upper Sharia Courts, Area Courts and Magistrate Courts, so the forum a case lands in is determined by the statute's own jurisdiction clause.

The inventory contains no Borno-specific arrest, raid, prosecution or killing of a transgender or gender-nonconforming person, and no documented execution under either Borno statute. The most recent source bearing on Borno's legal position is the UK Home Office note of June 2025.

Residents of Borno who are Muslim fall under the state's Sharia Penal Code Law 2001 as well as under the 2000 morality statute; the UK Home Office note of June 2025 records that Islamic law applies to Muslims in the twelve northern states and criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with death as the maximum penalty for 'sodomy' for men and penalties for 'lesbianism' ranging from death to flogging and imprisonment.

The 2000 statute's Section 7 death penalty applies on its own terms to same-gender intercourse, and Section 3 reaches lesbianism, a homosexual act, prostitution and pimping as state offences. Section 4 closed all brothels on commencement of the statute.

The hisbah operates as a morality police in the state, and the UK Home Office note of June 2025 treats the attitude of the hisbah as part of the enforcement environment for Shari'a provisions. Cases under the 2000 statute may be heard in the Upper Sharia Courts, the Area Courts or the Magistrate Courts under Section 9.

The Borno State Sharia Penal Code Law 2001 has no operation date or gazette identified in the sourcebook, and the text was obtained only in May 2006. Whether it has since been amended or replaced is unresolved in this inventory.

Whether the 2000 statute on prostitution, homosexuality, brothels and other sexual immoralities remains unamended and unrepealed as of the date of this record is unresolved; the inventory documents its enactment and gazettal but carries no later legislative action on it.

No Borno-specific enforcement incident, arrest, prosecution, assault or killing of a transgender or gender-nonconforming person is documented in this inventory, and no Borno-specific survey or statistic on such treatment is sourced.
